cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-commiss.summary: In the upper left corner a bust of Christ, haloed, appears in the sky; John sits below writing on a long scroll, and the seven angels of the churches stand among seven church buildings arranged across the page. The drawing visualises Christ's command to 'write the things which thou hast seen' and send them to the seven churches.
facts: The Trier Apocalypse contains 74 full-page drawings illustrating about 150 episodes of the Book of Revelation; it is one of the earliest illustrated Apocalypse manuscripts to survive.
Its pictures are thought to copy a late antique model of the 4th–6th century, which explains features such as books shown as scrolls and Christ as the beardless Logos.

cur:manuscripts-egberti-centurion.summary: Christ, haloed with a gold cross-nimbus, stands among his apostles and raises his hand toward the centurion, who approaches with his companions to ask healing for his servant. The calm dialogue of gestures carries the story of the centurion's faith.
facts: Egbert gave the book to the church of St Paulin in Trier, where it was used in services until the 18th century; it has been in the Trier city library since 1810 and was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2004 with other Reichenau manuscripts.
Seven of its miniatures are attributed to the anonymous 'Master of the Registrum Gregorii', who worked in Trier.

Q116246029.summary: Drawn in gold leaf on deep blue glass, a youthful figure in a tunic and mantle points a long rod at the objects beside him, the gesture with which early Christian art shows Christ working miracles. Small and intimate, this medallion carried the image of the wonder-working Christ into private devotion.
facts: The medallion is only about 2.5 cm across; the gold-leaf image was originally sealed between layers of glass.
The 'wand' held by Christ is a standard feature of 3rd–4th century miracle scenes, such as the raising of Lazarus, the multiplication of loaves and the miracle at Cana.
Q116246029.notes: Which miracle is shown is not certain from the image (the objects at left may be jars, suggesting Cana, but this is unconfirmed), so no specific passage is given. Scripture could be cited generally, e.g. John 2:11 (theme).

walters:44.301.summary: This crescent-shaped gold earring is edged with granulation and filigree loops and set with small bosses; at its centre a tiny cloisonné enamel medallion bears a bust of Christ. It was photographed with its companion earring (44.300), which shows the Virgin. Worn as personal jewellery, such pieces carried the holy images close to the body.
facts: The Walters lists the two earrings separately: 44.300 with a bust of the Virgin and 44.301 with Christ Pantokrator; both are dated to the 10th century.
Henry Walters bought them from the Paris dealer Henri Daguerre in 1926.
walters:44.301.notes: The only available photograph shows both earrings together; the enamel busts are only a few millimetres across and cannot be told apart clearly at this size. 'c' corrected from 'Orthodox' (a culture label) to the place of making.
